questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Purification: crystallization, sublimation, distillation, differential extraction and chromatography
questions.question: Which of the following compounds is purified by sublimation?

solution.key_concept: Sublimation purifies solids that pass directly from solid to vapour without melting.
steps: Sublimable solids include camphor, naphthalene, anthracene, benzoic acid and $I_2$.
Naphthalene is one of them, so it can be purified by sublimation.
solution.why_not_others: Glycerol is purified by reduced-pressure distillation. Aniline is purified by steam distillation. Chloroform is a liquid separated by simple distillation.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that any volatile compound sublimes. Only certain solids pass directly into vapour.
solution.time_saving_tip: Memorise the five standard sublimable solids: camphor, naphthalene, anthracene, benzoic acid and iodine.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Purification: crystallization, sublimation, distillation, differential extraction and chromatography
questions.question: A mixture of o-nitrophenol and p-nitrophenol is best separated by

solution.key_concept: Steam distillation separates steam-volatile, water-immiscible compounds from non-volatile ones.
steps: o-Nitrophenol has intramolecular H-bonding, which makes it steam volatile.
p-Nitrophenol is not steam volatile, so it stays behind in the flask.
Steam distillation therefore separates the two isomers.
solution.why_not_others: Simple distillation needs liquids with very different boiling points. Reduced-pressure distillation is for liquids that decompose below their boiling points, such as glycerol. Sublimation applies to solids such as camphor or naphthalene.
solution.common_trap: Confusing steam distillation with reduced-pressure distillation, since both work below the normal boiling point.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Purification: crystallization, sublimation, distillation, differential extraction and chromatography
questions.question: In a TLC experiment, the solvent front moves 12.0 cm from the base line and a component moves 4.8 cm from the base line. The $R_f$ value of the component is

solution.key_concept: $R_f$ = distance moved by the substance divided by the distance moved by the solvent, both measured from the base line.
steps: $R_f = 0.40$, which is less than 1 as expected.
solution.why_not_others: 2.50 inverts the ratio, which is impossible because $R_f < 1$. 0.60 is $1 - R_f$. 0.29 wrongly divides by the sum $4.8 + 12.0$.
solution.common_trap: Inverting the ratio. $R_f$ can never exceed 1.
solution.time_saving_tip: Check that your answer is below 1 before marking it.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Purification: crystallization, sublimation, distillation, differential extraction and chromatography
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: In steam distillation, aniline distils at a temperature below 373 K.
statements.R: In steam distillation, the mixture boils when the sum of the vapour pressures of water and the organic liquid equals atmospheric pressure.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: In steam distillation, $p = p_{water} + p_{organic} = p_{atm}$.
steps: Water and aniline each contribute vapour pressure.
Their total reaches atmospheric pressure before water alone would, that is, before 373 K.
So aniline distils below 373 K. R is true and it explains A.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are true, and the vapour-pressure sum is exactly why the temperature stays below 373 K. So options (2), (3) and (4) are wrong.
solution.common_trap: Thinking aniline must reach its own boiling point of 457 K to distil.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Purification: crystallization, sublimation, distillation, differential extraction and chromatography
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: In thin layer chromatography, the component with the higher $R_f$ value is the one more strongly adsorbed on the stationary phase.
statements.II: In paper chromatography, water held in the paper acts as the stationary phase, and separation occurs by partition.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: A larger $R_f$ means weaker adsorption. Paper chromatography is partition chromatography.
steps: A weakly adsorbed component moves farther, so it has the higher $R_f$. Statement I is incorrect.
In paper chromatography, water held in the paper is the stationary phase, and separation is by partition. Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
solution.why_not_others: Statement I reverses the relation between $R_f$ and adsorption, which rules out options (1) and (3). Statement II is true, which rules out option (2).
solution.common_trap: Linking a higher $R_f$ with stronger adsorption.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Qualitative analysis: detection of nitrogen, sulphur, phosphorus and halogens
questions.question: In Lassaigne's test, the presence of nitrogen is confirmed when the sodium fusion extract, treated with $FeSO_4$ followed by conc. $H_2SO_4$, gives

solution.key_concept: $NaCN$ in the extract forms ferrocyanide, which then forms Prussian blue.
steps: $6CN^- + Fe^{2+} \rightarrow [Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}$
$3[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-} + 4Fe^{3+} \rightarrow Fe_4[Fe(CN)_6]_3 \cdot xH_2O$, which is Prussian blue.
solution.why_not_others: A black precipitate ($PbS$) and a violet colour (with nitroprusside) are tests for sulphur. A yellow precipitate with ammonium molybdate is the test for phosphorus.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the sulphur colour tests with the nitrogen test.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Qualitative analysis: detection of nitrogen, sulphur, phosphorus and halogens
questions.question: Which of the following nitrogen-containing compounds gives a negative Lassaigne's test for nitrogen?

solution.key_concept: Nitrogen is detected as $CN^-$, so the compound must contain carbon as well as nitrogen.
steps: Hydrazine, $NH_2NH_2$, contains no carbon.
Without carbon, no $NaCN$ forms during fusion, so no Prussian blue appears.
solution.why_not_others: Aniline, urea and glycine all contain both C and N, so they form $NaCN$ and give a positive test.
solution.common_trap: Assuming every nitrogen compound gives Prussian blue.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Qualitative analysis: detection of nitrogen, sulphur, phosphorus and halogens
questions.question: Before $AgNO_3$ is added to test for halogens, the sodium fusion extract is boiled with dilute $HNO_3$ in order to
options: oxidise the halide ions to free halogens
convert the halide ions into hydrogen halides that react faster with $AgNO_3$
decompose $NaCN$ and $Na_2S$, which would otherwise precipitate as $AgCN$ and $Ag_2S$
precipitate any phosphorus present as phosphate

solution.key_concept: Cyanide and sulphide ions interfere with the silver nitrate test.
steps: If N or S is present, the extract contains $CN^-$ and $S^{2-}$.
These would precipitate as $AgCN$ and $Ag_2S$, giving a false result.
Boiling with $HNO_3$ destroys them first.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): decompose $NaCN$ and $Na_2S$, which would otherwise precipitate as $AgCN$ and $Ag_2S$
solution.why_not_others: The halide must stay as $X^-$ to precipitate as $AgX$, so oxidising it would defeat the test. Reaction speed is not the purpose. Phosphorus is tested separately, using $Na_2O_2$ and molybdate.
solution.common_trap: Adding $AgNO_3$ directly to the extract.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Qualitative analysis: detection of nitrogen, sulphur, phosphorus and halogens
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: A
list_I.text: Sodium fusion extract treated with $FeSO_4$, then conc. $H_2SO_4$ (N present)

list_I.label: B
list_I.text: Sodium fusion extract treated with sodium nitroprusside (S present)

list_I.label: C
list_I.text: Extract prepared with insufficient sodium, treated with $Fe^{3+}$ (N and S present)

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Compound heated with $Na_2O_2$, then boiled with $HNO_3$ and ammonium molybdate (P present)

solution.key_concept: Each element gives a characteristic colour in the qualitative tests.
steps: N gives Prussian blue: A-IV.
S with nitroprusside gives a violet colour: B-III.
$NaSCN$ with $Fe^{3+}$ gives blood-red $[Fe(SCN)]^{2+}$: C-I.
P gives a yellow ammonium phosphomolybdate precipitate: D-II.
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) swaps the violet and blood-red colours. Option (2) gives Prussian blue to sulphur. Option (3) swaps the thiocyanate and phosphorus results.
solution.common_trap: Assigning blood red to sulphur alone. It comes from $SCN^-$, so it needs both N and S.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Qualitative analysis: detection of nitrogen, sulphur, phosphorus and halogens
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the detection of elements in organic compounds are correct?

statements.B: With excess sodium, $NaSCN$ is decomposed into $NaCN$ and $Na_2S$, so the blood-red colour is not obtained even if N and S are both present.
statements.C: Diazonium salts reliably give Prussian blue in Lassaigne's test.
statements.D: For phosphorus, the compound is heated with $Na_2O_2$ to oxidise phosphorus to phosphate.
statements.E: Sulphide ions give a black precipitate of $PbS$ with lead acetate in acetic acid.

options: A, B, D and E only

solution.key_concept: Know the colour reactions and the exceptions in Lassaigne's test.
steps: A: true. $AgCl$ is white and soluble in $NH_4OH$.
B: true. $NaSCN + 2Na \rightarrow NaCN + Na_2S$, so separate N and S tests are seen.
C: false. Diazonium salts lose $N_2$ on heating and fail the test.
D and E: true.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A, B, D and E only
solution.why_not_others: Options (2) and (3) include the false statement C. Option (1) leaves out the true statements D and E.
solution.common_trap: Believing every compound with N and S always gives blood red, or that every N compound gives Prussian blue.
solution.time_saving_tip: Spot C as false first; that eliminates two options at once.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Quantitative analysis (basic principles): C, H, N, halogens, S and P
questions.question: In Liebig's method for estimating carbon and hydrogen, the carbon dioxide produced is absorbed in

solution.key_concept: In Liebig's method, $H_2O$ is absorbed in anhydrous $CaCl_2$ and $CO_2$ in $KOH$.
steps: The compound is burnt with $CuO$.
Water is trapped by $CaCl_2$, and $CO_2$ is trapped by $KOH$. Each is then weighed.
solution.why_not_others: $CaCl_2$ absorbs water, not $CO_2$. $CuO$ is the oxidant. Copper gauze reduces oxides of nitrogen in Dumas' method.
solution.common_trap: Swapping the roles of $CaCl_2$ and $KOH$.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Quantitative analysis (basic principles): C, H, N, halogens, S and P
questions.question: In a Carius determination, 0.250 g of an organic bromo compound gave 0.376 g of $AgBr$. The percentage of bromine in the compound is (Ag = 108, Br = 80)

solution.key_concept: $\%Br = \frac{80}{188} \times \frac{m_{AgBr}}{m} \times 100$
steps: Moles of $AgBr = \frac{0.376}{188} = 0.002$
Mass of Br $= 0.002 \times 80 = 0.160$ g
solution.why_not_others: 86.4% uses the mass of Ag (108) instead of Br. 36.0% is $100 - 64$. 83.8% uses the molar mass of $AgCl$ (143.5) in place of $AgBr$.
solution.common_trap: Using the wrong silver halide molar mass, or the mass of Ag instead of the halogen.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Quantitative analysis (basic principles): C, H, N, halogens, S and P
questions.question: In a Kjeldahl estimation, the ammonia from 1.00 g of an organic compound was passed into 50 mL of 0.5 M $H_2SO_4$. The excess acid required 60 mL of 0.5 M $NaOH$ for neutralisation. The percentage of nitrogen in the compound is

solution.key_concept: $\%N = \frac{1.4 \times N_{acid} \times V_{acid\,used}}{m}$, where the acid used is found by back-titration.
steps: Since 0.5 M $H_2SO_4$ = 1 N, the acid taken is $50 \times 1 = 50$ meq.
Excess acid = $60 \times 0.5 = 30$ meq, so the acid used by $NH_3$ = 20 meq.
solution.why_not_others: 42.0% uses the back-titration value (30 meq) as the acid used. 14.0% treats $H_2SO_4$ as 0.5 N. 70.0% uses the total acid taken (50 meq).
solution.common_trap: Forgetting that 0.5 M $H_2SO_4$ is 1 N.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Quantitative analysis (basic principles): C, H, N, halogens, S and P
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: Kjeldahl's method cannot be used to estimate the nitrogen in pyridine.
statements.R: In Kjeldahl's method, the nitrogen of the compound is converted into $N_2$ gas, whose volume is measured.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Kjeldahl's method converts N to $(NH_4)_2SO_4$ and fails for nitrogen in a ring.
steps: Ring nitrogen, as in pyridine, is not converted to $(NH_4)_2SO_4$, so A is true.
Converting N to $N_2$ and measuring its volume is Dumas' method, so R is false.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A is true but R is false
solution.why_not_others: R describes Dumas' method, not Kjeldahl's, so options (1), (2) and (4) are wrong.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the Dumas and Kjeldahl methods.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Quantitative analysis (basic principles): C, H, N, halogens, S and P
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: In Dumas' method, the nitrogen collected over $KOH$ solution is moist, so the aqueous tension is subtracted from the observed pressure before the volume is converted to STP.
statements.II: In a Carius estimation, 0.320 g of an organic compound gave 0.466 g of $BaSO_4$, which corresponds to 20% sulphur in the compound.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Correct the Dumas gas pressure for aqueous tension, and use $\%S = \frac{32}{233} \times \frac{m_{BaSO_4}}{m} \times 100$.
steps: Statement I: the gas is moist, so the pressure of dry $N_2$ = observed pressure minus aqueous tension. Correct.
Statement II: moles of $BaSO_4 = \frac{0.466}{233} = 0.002$, so the mass of S is $0.064$ g.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are verified as true, so options (2), (3) and (4) are wrong.
solution.common_trap: Using the moist gas pressure directly in the Dumas calculation.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Calculation of empirical and molecular formulae
questions.question: Which pair of compounds has the same empirical formula?

solution.key_concept: The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms.
steps: Glucose, $C_6H_{12}O_6$, reduces to $CH_2O$.
Acetic acid, $C_2H_4O_2$, also reduces to $CH_2O$.
solution.why_not_others: Benzene is CH but ethene ($C_2H_4$) is $CH_2$. Acetylene is CH but ethane ($C_2H_6$) is $CH_3$. Formaldehyde is $CH_2O$ but methanol is $CH_4O$.
solution.common_trap: Matching compounds by the number of carbon atoms instead of by the atom ratio.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Calculation of empirical and molecular formulae
questions.question: An organic compound contains 40.0% C and 6.67% H, the rest being oxygen. Its vapour density is 90. The molecular formula of the compound is

solution.key_concept: Use the empirical formula with $M = 2 \times VD$ and $n = M / \text{EF mass}$.
steps: Relative moles: C = 3.33, H = 6.67, O = 3.33, giving a ratio of 1 : 2 : 1, so the empirical formula is $CH_2O$ (mass 30).
solution.why_not_others: $CH_2O$ is only the empirical formula. $C_3H_6O_3$ wrongly takes the vapour density (90) as the molar mass. $C_2H_4O_2$ corresponds to a molar mass of 60.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting to double the vapour density.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Calculation of empirical and molecular formulae
questions.question: A compound contains 40.91% C and 4.55% H, the rest being oxygen. Its molar mass is 176 g mol$^{-1}$. Its molecular formula is

solution.key_concept: Do not round 1.33; multiply all the ratios by 3.
steps: Relative moles: C = 3.41, H = 4.55, O = 3.41, giving a ratio of 1 : 1.33 : 1.
Multiplying by 3 gives the empirical formula $C_3H_4O_3$ (mass 88).
$n = 176/88 = 2$, so the molecular formula is $C_6H_8O_6$.
solution.why_not_others: $C_3H_4O_3$ is only the empirical formula. $C_6H_6O_6$ comes from rounding 1.33 down to 1. $C_6H_9O_6$ comes from treating 1.33 as 1.5.
solution.common_trap: Rounding 1.33 to the nearest integer or to 1.5.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Calculation of empirical and molecular formulae
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: A
list_I.text: Empirical formula $CH_2O$, molar mass 60 g mol$^{-1}$

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Empirical formula $CH$, molar mass 26 g mol$^{-1}$

solution.key_concept: $n = M / \text{EF mass}$, with $M = 2 \times VD$.
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) uses the vapour density values as molar masses. Option (3) swaps benzene and acetylene. Option (4) mismatches the empirical formulas.
solution.common_trap: Taking the vapour density as the molar mass.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Calculation of empirical and molecular formulae
questions.question: Which of the following statements about empirical and molecular formulae are correct?

statements.A: A compound with vapour density 23 has a molar mass of 46 g mol$^{-1}$.
statements.B: If the relative mole ratio C : H is 1 : 1.5, the empirical formula is $C_2H_3$.
statements.C: Formaldehyde and acetic acid have the same molecular formula.
statements.D: The multiplier n that converts an empirical formula into a molecular formula can be a fraction such as 1.5.
statements.E: When the percentage of oxygen is not given, it must be found by difference before the relative moles are calculated.

options: A, C, D and E only

solution.key_concept: Apply the rules: $M = 2 \times VD$, fractional ratios are multiplied up, n is a whole number, and %O is found by difference.
steps: A: $2 \times 23 = 46$. True.
B: multiplying 1 : 1.5 by 2 gives $C_2H_3$. True.
C: they share only the empirical formula $CH_2O$; their molecular formulas differ. False.
D: n must be a whole number. False. E: true.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): A, B and E only
solution.why_not_others: Option (2) includes the false statement D. Option (3) includes the false statement C. Option (4) includes both C and D.
solution.common_trap: Confusing the same empirical formula with the same molecular formula.
solution.time_saving_tip: Spot C and D as false first; that eliminates options (2), (3) and (4).

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Numerical problems in organic quantitative analysis
questions.question: In the Carius method, 0.20 g of an organic compound gives 0.287 g of $AgCl$. What is the percentage of chlorine in the compound?

solution.key_concept: In gravimetric estimation, the mass of the element equals the mass of precipitate multiplied by the mass fraction of the element in it. For Cl in $AgCl$ this fraction is 35.5/143.5.
solution.why_not_others: 17.75% and 71.0% come from wrongly halving or doubling the correct value. 61.1% comes from using the bromine fraction 80/188 instead of 35.5/143.5.
solution.common_trap: Using the wrong precipitate fraction, such as the one for $AgBr$, or mishandling the factor for chlorine.
solution.time_saving_tip: 0.287/143.5 = 0.002 mol exactly, so the mass of Cl is $0.002 \times 35.5 = 0.071$ g.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Numerical problems in organic quantitative analysis
questions.question: In Dumas method, 0.25 g of an organic compound gives 30 mL of moist nitrogen collected at 300 K and 787 mm Hg. The aqueous tension at 300 K is 27 mm Hg. What is the percentage of nitrogen in the compound?

solution.key_concept: First subtract the aqueous tension from the observed pressure. Then convert the dry gas volume to STP, where 28 g of $N_2$ occupies 22400 mL.
steps: Pressure of dry $N_2$ = 787 - 27 = 760 mm Hg.
$V_{STP} = \frac{760 \times 30 \times 273}{760 \times 300} = 27.3$ mL.
solution.why_not_others: 14.13% results from using 787 mm Hg without subtracting the aqueous tension. 15.00% results from using 30 mL directly, without converting to STP. 27.30% results from taking 14 g of nitrogen per 22400 mL instead of 28 g.
solution.common_trap: Using the moist gas pressure directly instead of subtracting the aqueous tension.
solution.time_saving_tip: The dry pressure is exactly 760 mm Hg, so only the temperature correction (273/300) is needed.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Numerical problems in organic quantitative analysis
questions.question: In Kjeldahl's method, the ammonia evolved from 0.40 g of an organic compound is absorbed in 50 mL of 0.1 M $H_2SO_4$. The unreacted acid requires 60 mL of 0.1 M $NaOH$ for complete neutralisation. What is the percentage of nitrogen in the compound?

solution.key_concept: The acid used by $NH_3$ equals the total acid minus the acid neutralised by $NaOH$. Since $H_2SO_4$ is dibasic, 1 M $H_2SO_4$ = 2 N.
steps: Total acid = $50 \times 0.1 \times 2 = 10$ milliequivalents.
Acid neutralised by $NaOH$ = $60 \times 0.1 = 6$ milliequivalents.
Acid used by $NH_3$ = 4 milliequivalents. This corresponds to $4 \times 14 = 56$ mg of N.
%N = $\frac{0.056}{0.40} \times 100 = 14\%$. The formula $\frac{1.4 \times 0.1 \times 2(50 - 30)}{0.40}$ gives the same result.
solution.why_not_others: 7% comes from omitting the factor 2 for dibasic $H_2SO_4$ in the formula. 35% comes from ignoring the back titration. 28% comes from using 28 instead of 14 per milliequivalent of nitrogen.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting that $H_2SO_4$ is dibasic, or forgetting to subtract the acid neutralised by $NaOH$.
solution.time_saving_tip: Work in milliequivalents: 10 - 6 = 4, so the mass of N is 56 mg.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Numerical problems in organic quantitative analysis
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: A sample of nitrogen collected over water at 273 K and a total pressure of 760 mm Hg occupies a larger volume than the same amount of dry nitrogen at STP.
statements.R: In Dumas method, the aqueous tension is added to the observed pressure to obtain the pressure of dry nitrogen.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: The pressure of dry $N_2$ equals the observed pressure minus the aqueous tension: $p_1 = p - f$.
steps: In the moist sample, $N_2$ exerts only (760 - f) mm Hg, which is less than 760 mm Hg.
At the same temperature and amount of gas, a lower pressure means a larger volume, so A is true.
The aqueous tension is subtracted from the observed pressure, not added, so R is false.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A is true but R is false
solution.why_not_others: R is false, so options (1) and (2) are ruled out. A is correct, so option (4) is ruled out.
solution.common_trap: Adding the aqueous tension, or ignoring it altogether.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Numerical problems in organic quantitative analysis
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: In the Carius method, 0.40 g of an organic compound gives 0.466 g of $BaSO_4$, so the percentage of sulphur in the compound is 13.7%.
statements.II: A compound containing 54.5% carbon and 9.1% hydrogen, the rest being oxygen, has the empirical formula $C_2H_4O$.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: %S is found as $\frac{32}{233} \times \frac{\text{mass of } BaSO_4}{\text{mass of compound}} \times 100$. An empirical formula comes from mole ratios after finding oxygen by difference.
steps: Mass of S = $0.466 \times \frac{32}{233} = 0.064$ g, so %S = $\frac{0.064}{0.40} \times 100 = 16\%$. Statement I is incorrect.
The 13.7% value comes from dividing 0.064 by the precipitate mass (0.466 g) instead of the compound mass.
For Statement II, %O = 100 - 54.5 - 9.1 = 36.4.
Mole ratios are C : H : O = 54.5/12 : 9.1/1 : 36.4/16 = 4.54 : 9.1 : 2.275, which simplifies to 2 : 4 : 1. Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
solution.why_not_others: Statement I gives a wrong %S (the correct value is 16%), which rules out options (1) and (3). Statement II is verified as correct, which rules out option (2).
solution.common_trap: Dividing by the precipitate mass instead of the compound mass. Another trap is forgetting to find oxygen by difference.
solution.time_saving_tip: 0.466/233 = 0.002 mol, so the mass of S is $0.002 \times 32 = 0.064$ g.
